about. There is another peculiarity about this shovel that was not found in the rod of the great statesman and leader of ancient days. I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, what that peculiarity is, so that you and I may understand it. Will you permit me to tell a story about a man who sold a coach dog, that is a dog with spots of black and white. This coach dog was sold, and when it went out into the rain the man who bought it discovered that there was some fraud about it, that the spots which were black had become white and that the white spots had become black. The new owner of the dog, feeling very badly about it, went to the man who had . sold it to him and said, " What sort of dog is this? it has all gone to <pot, and is no good." " Oh," said the man, " I forgot to tell you 'that an umbrella goes with that dog." He had sold the dog without the umbrella. Now, about this shovel with the hole in it, which is the great wand by which the Minister of Militia and Defence performs all his miracles-let me tell you that it is a well understood thing that a woman goes with this shovel. There is a hole in the shovel so that the minister may look through and see the woman. It is impossible to use the one without the other, and in that way this shovel is a companionable sort of article which performs wonderful things with its proper concomitants. Of all the discoveries that our good friend has made, there is none really different from the mass of ordinary humdrum business connected with the running of a department except this shovel, and I waited with the greatest patience, and looked very closely at the minister, to see if he would give us some account of this shovel, or of what goes with it; but I am sorry to say we were not enlightened upon the subject.
'These, Sir, are some of the great achievements of this great man who will not for a moment condescend to listen to one of the ordinary members of the House. I am pleased, not sorry, to say that on this side of the House, possibly with very few exceptions, we are ordinary people with ordinary common sense, who represent the ordinary brain and brawn and business of this country. We were told that there were no politics in the department, but, Mr. Speaker, let me put to you in the form of a few questions, some things that were put up to the minister, and let me point out to you that when these matters were put up to him he was aware that the affairs of his department were not being [Mi-. McKenzie.]
conducted as they ought to be. I am now going to quote from a letter put upon Hansard by the Prime Minister on April 15, 1915, a letter which gives us an idea and a clear understanding of the fact that at all events from that date the Minister of Militia and Defence had knowledge of the fact that things were not regarded as being right in his department. On page 2611, volume 3, of the Debates of 1915, we find this letter:
Ottawa, November 18, 1915.
Dear General Hughes,-When acting as Minister of Militia during, your absence at Val-cartier I instructed Colonel Fiset,, Deputy Minister, that the use of outside agents and middlemen should be avoided and that contracts should be made directly with manufacturers so that any unnecessary commissions or increased prices might be avoided. This is undoubtedly the wise policy and is entirely in accordance with the principles laid down by our party during the years past. If for any good reason you may think it desirable in the public interest that a different course should be pursued in any particular instance by reason of conditions arising out of the war I hope that you will first consult me as I consider the principle to be of prime importance.
Yours faithfully,
R. L. Borden.
Major General,
The Hon. Sam Hughes,
Minister of Militia,
Ottawa, Ont.
That, Sir, was on the 18th November, 1914, after the Prime Minister had had an opportunity of presiding over the Militia Department for a short time, and, no doubt, of learning for himself the condition of things in that department. Six months afterwards, while the department was still, of course, under the control of the same minister, and after he had been told that things were not going right, we find a strong Conservative coming down to this House with a report upon the affairs of that department which says:
In* view of the evidence adduced during the course of their inquiry into the matters referred by the House to them, your committee desire to draw the attention of the House to the requirement for the inauguration of a system of purchase, inspection and audit that will adequately protect the country from irregu-1 larities and frauds.
That, Sir, is the condition which had prevailed six months after the Prime Minister had warned the Minister of Militia that things were not going right in his department. A like report was brought down from the Public Accounts Committee. It had been moved by the hon. member for Kingston and carried unanimously in a committee which had an overwhelming majority of the supporters of the minister

and of the Government. That shows that six months after the warning he had received it was absolutely impossible for the gentleman at the head of the department to get things straight.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I was going to put to you, in the form of a few questions, certain propositions that came before the Minister of Militia and Defence in regard to the running of his department. After he had received the warning which I read a moment ago he was asked by his party heelers: " Can we send the soldiers to the trenches with improperly made shoes, practically with paper shoes, and with bare feet?" The answer was: " iSo far as the department is concerned, yes, if you can make money out of it, and can conceal it,
I have no objection." "Can we send our soldiers to the front with horses with heelspring, horses that are spavined, horses that are blind, horses that are ring-boned, horses that are winded-can we send such horses as those for service with our troops?" "Yes, so far as General Hughes is concerned, if you can manage to do it without being found out." "Can we send the boys to the front with defective and treacherous field glasses that cannot be depended upon?"
" Certainly, if you can get away with it; I will stand behind you as far as I can protect you in doing it." That is what happened in so far as these things are concerned. As we heard here last night, the question is naturally put: can we take a monopoly of the hay and oats required in any province of the Dominion of Canada, fix the price just to suit ourselves, take the farmer by the throat, take his goods whether he likes it or not and sell at our own price at the most extraordinary profit we can make? Can you stand by that and will you stand behind it? That has been done, and we have not heard a murmur from any member of the Government saying that the thing was wrong. That is what is being done to-day in the province of New Brunswick and I have no doubt in other provinces all over the country. The most extraordinary thing is that they feel called upon to fix the price for the farmer so that the farmer cannot get anything but what they are pleased to give him. After commandeering his hay at a starvation price, Tory heelers ask and receive at the hands of this Government the right of monopolizing the traffic in this country so that this hay cannot be sold in any other province or in any place outside of the Dominion except as it may please the Government to permit
the farmers to do it. This is a most extraordinary condition of things and a state of affairs that was never known to have existed anywhere else, or under any government, except the Government which is presided over by the present Prime Minister and under the department with which I am dealing particularly at the present time, presided over by the hon. gentleman who has addressed us this afternoon.
In so far as the management of that department is concerned, it could not be worse than it is. There is not a thing upon which they put their hands but they leave the ear-marks of mismanagement and the ear-marks of what appears to the ordinary looker-on as dishonesty and lack of proper business principles. When this Government comes to this House, or goes to the country, and asks for a further lease of power, they are presuming to a most extraordinary degree upon the patience of the people of Canada. The war question is the paramount question, and the people of Canada, and the people of Nova Scotia, for whom I speak most particularly at the present moment, will be united in the desire to place at the disposal of the Government everything that can be used for the promotion of the war and the final and ultimate success of the Allies. But it is putting the patience, the endurance, and the loyalty of the people to the most extraordinary test when you ask to be permitted to extend the principal beyond those proper constitutional limits which should govern the management of the affairs of the country.
I pointed out a few minutes ago, and I point out again, that no minister of the Crown can come to this House and say that he never knew about wrong doing in his department until it was brought out by the Public Accounts Committee. He certainly did not, and he certainly got his contract from the minister. Will anybody tell me that the minister did not know that he was the member for Carleton? Well, he has evidently been disgraced in the eyes of some decent people, because there are some decent people in New Brunswick. I wish to say a little in regard to the partyism which has been rampant in this country since the Conservatives came into power in 1911, and to point out that, in so far as my part of the country is concerned, this Government has been to us a disappointment. We had laid out for ourselves certain schemes, and it was the policy of the Administration of Sir Wilfred Laurier that large developments in railway matters should be brought about in our part oi the country so that our fisheries and our farming industry and all our other large industries should be put in touch with the heart pulsations of this country- A railway policy was adopted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Government for the province o' Nova Scotia, but I am sorry to say that with the exception of that part of the road which is in the constituency of the present Premier, everything else was cut out. I am sure that the Premier himself cannot be to proud of this matter. For years before 1911 the hon. member for Pie-tou (Mr. Macdonald), the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), and all the members for the island of Cape Breton, including myself were pulling on the same oar with the then leader of the Opposition for the obtaining of better railway facilities in the eastern part of the Maritime Provinces. While our railway was to be built, his railway was to be built as well; but when the wheel of fortune turned and we had no further say as to the expenditure of money, the present Prime Minister built his own railway and pitched us over the side of the boat into the sea and would not look at us at all. That is not a very big way for a big man to deal with a question of such importance to us and to our people.

We were told by Conservatives at that time that they would build the railroad that we were to have, but one year, two years, three years, four years have passed and the fifth year is passing and nothing has been done. They do not intend to do anything and nothing will be done until the Liberals come back into power. It would not be so bad if our friends had been saving the money, if it could be said that although they were not building the rail-5 p.m. ways for us, the money was in the treasury. We left them with all bills paid, everything squared up and the finanoes of the country in first-class condition. To show you, Sir, in how excellent a condition the finances were, I simply refer to the first Budget speech delivered by Sir Thomas White when he became Minister of Finance. We were told by the present Prime Minister, a few months before our friends came into power, that an expenditure of something like $87,000,000 was the clearest evidence of dishonesty and v misappropriation of the money of the people of this country, and that, if they came into power, they could run the country with much less money and show better results for it. If the Prime Minister had been in earnest about that, we should have had some evidence of it when he came into power, and that evidence would be that he would reduce the expenditure. What do we find? The first year our friends were in power, the expenditure was $98,000,000, or 11,000,000 more than this horrible expenditure of which the Prime Minister spoke. The second year the expenditure was $112,000,000, or $25,000,000 of an increase. The next year the expenditure was $127,000,000, or $40,000,000 of an increase, and the fourth and last year of which we have an account the expenditure was $140,000,000, or $53,000,000 of an increase. That shows that the expenditure was growing by leaps and hounds, and that the Government was absolutely regardless of the promise of retrenchment that we had heard so much about a few years ago.
What about the interest charges? When we came into power in 1896 the interest expenditure of this country was $10,000,000. We went out of office in 1911, the interest expenditure was only $12,000,000, or an annual increase during the fifteen years of the Laurier Administration of $135,337. The interest expenditure, or the interest appropriation for the last year of which we have an account, that is so far as the ordinary expenditure is concerned, outside of war

expenditure, was $21,'500,000, or a yearly increase since the Conservative party came into power of ?3,166,000, and this expenditure is getting worse instead of better as time goes on.
It is up to us all to put all our energies together in order to put an end to this war, to do all that we can as a great country, to put forth all our resources of men and money in order to bring about a victorious ending to this struggle. But let us not forget and let not the people of this country forget the conditions which prevail to-day in British Columbia, in Manitoba, in Prince Edward Island, and in New Brunswick, or wherever else the Tories have sway in this country. We must not forget that our great duty is not only to bring back to power the leader of the Opposition, who is the old political physician in this country, but to bring back the conditions, both financial and moral, which he created in this country, and which no other party than that of which he is the leader is capable of restoring and perpetuating in this great country of ours.

Mr. Speaker, you will permit me, in rising to speak on, the motion for am Address to His Royal Highness the Governor General in reply to the speech from the Throne, to join with the other members of this House in congratulating you upon your being elevated to the office which you now occupy. I am not a very old member of this House, but I have had the pleasure of sitting under the administration of three Speakers. I think that those of us who sat in the House during that length of time realize, as I do, that the task of the Speaker is not by any means easy; that it calls for qualities of an exceptionally high character; that it calls not only for great tact and great impartiality, but for great firmness as well. Upon many occasions these qualities have been tested to the very uttermost, and it is inspiring to find in the young democracy of Canada, where we are carrying on institutions British in character, that under those tests the Canadian character has risen to the, same level as that of their Anglo-Saxon forebears, and that democracy has held its own in the conduct of the affairs of this House.
I wish also to congratulate the mover of the Address, the hon. member from the far West (Mr. Alfred Thompson), and the seconder, the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Eugene Paquet). I was particularly glad that the hon. member for the Yukon had the honour of moving the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. I myself am a western man, and, as the northern part of my constituency touches that great country from which the member for Yukon comes, naturally we have a good many things in common, and, perhaps, look at national questions at a different angle from that of other members who have not been familiar with the West.
I noted with a great deal of interest the length at which hon. gentlemen dealt with the question of the war, which, after all, occupier, our thoughts to the exclusion of almost everything else at this time. I suppose there is not a member in this House, from the leader of the Government to the leader of the Opposition and down to the youngest member, who does not feel, in common with the rest of the people of this country, the presence of the shadow of this great conflict. I think that every waking moment of our lives is to some extent affected by the grave and tragic character of the struggle that is now going on. My light hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in opening his remarks, observed that we meet again under the shadow of this disastrous war. We unquestionably do, and it is, perhaps, a sad feature of our democratic life and of our party government that we lay too much stress on -these -smaller affairs of party interest, to the neglect of the paramount issue that is before the Canadian people at the present time. The morning after war was declared, I happened to be in the c-ity of Vancouver, that beautiful, far-western province with which so many members of the House are familiar. It -so happened that the Prime Minister had asked me to address a convention of Canadian Clubs; it was on August 5. War was declared late in the night of August 4, and I reached Vancouver the night before. I am not likely to forget the deep emotion that stirred all those -people on that occasion. I am not likely to forget the wave of passion- that swept over every man and woman present, or the profound conviction that these people had as to the underlying justice of the -cause which had at last -driven Great Britain into the war on the side of the Allies. Nor am 1 likely to forget the determination that moved every heart and every mind, out in that far-western province, to stay with this thing and to see it through, no matter what it

might cost. It was with a recollection of this incident, which would naturally burn itself into one's brain, that I watched with ithe deepest sympathy and the deepest pride the generous response that was made by our far-western country when the Empire called for their support in this great struggle. I recall many instances of men in my own constituency in the far north who walked twenty, even thirty and forty miles from distant and isolated sections of the country in order that they might be on hand at the earliest possible moment to answer the call. I remember one typical instance: that of a man, living in one of the beautiful valleys in the northern part of British Columbia. He was English by birth; he had been in the country a great many years, and had finally built his house, developed his small farm, and arrived at the point where he expected to get some little comfort from his labours and some little enjoyment from his life. His mother was still alive; his father was not. His mother *had three sons in the war: one in the navy and two in the army. Not very long after the outbreak of war she wrote her son that one of his brothers had been wounded and another killed, and that she thought the hour had struck when he too should take his turn. He did not hesitate. He packed the few small things that he wished to take with him on his journey, nailed fast the door of his small house, took the train and answered the call, believing that he was fulfilling the highest duties of a British subject in his country's hour of trial. It is that spirit, fSir, that has dominated the people of the West generally in regard to the call which was so strong and which came with such sudden and terrific force. The fact that they responded to that call and that they responded to it in that spirit is the best .guarantee of the final outcome of this war.
I should be a very poor Canadian if 1 did not share the pride of those who are living in eastern and central Canada that the response which I have described in the far West was also made, with equal vigour and equal patriotism, throughout the length and breadth of the eastern country. Certainly, if there should be any inspiration to those of us who are not at the front to do our duty here, it should be the feeling that those men have given up everything they possess in the world-home, comforts, even honourable and distinguished positions-in order that they might fight our battles. I have seen these

men march through the city of Ottawa; it has been my pleasure to be present on many occasions, especially when the western divisions have gone through, when the Duke of Connaught, whom we are all so delighted to have with us in this time of stress, and the hon. Minister of Militia, were present to review the troops. I have seen scores of personal friends amongst them; I have watched their career. I have, as every man in	this House
has, lost by death	in the	battle
trenches many a warm personal friend. I have known others who were wounded, and some have returned. It has been an immense satisfaction to a man from my province, who has known these men, not only to watch the response that they made, but to see that they have borne themselves not only as we would expect a Canadian to bear himself, but in such a way as to line up with the very finest traditions of the whole Empire. I do not dwell on these things, because it was not for that purpose that I rose to speak. My hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. McKenzie) will perhaps pardon me if I do not allude to the matter he has given us in the last hour. I found it, I confess, a little bit mixed. He was talking about chaos, and the sun and stars and military shovels, and the iniquities of the Conservative Administrations in Manitoba, New Brunswick and British Columbia, and the rampant partyism that has been observable in this country since the unfortunate hour when the Conservatives assumed office in Ottawa. I think, perhaps, we can take all that for what it is worth; at least my hon. friend will not think I am discourteous to him if I do not touch on the matter which he produced just now. No man could take any exception to the tone of a good many of the speeches that have been delivered. No man could take exception to the tone of the speech of the rigid, hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) or that of my hon. friend from the West who sits behind him (Mr. Michael Clark), or those of several other hon gentlemen opposite. It is true that some of those speeches have contained a goi d deal of criticism of things in connection with which we must expect criticism. I do not know that any man can object to having strong and keen criticism levelled against him, when he is placed in a position of ie-sponsibility, as members of a government are. Nobody will complain of that. But I think, also, we can realize that there is a good deal of criticism that is expressed, and a certain amount of criticism has been

heard in this debate, which is not of a helpful character, but is entirely designed to make political capital for the man who advances it. The suggestion that the recruiting meetings addressed by members of this Government and others on this side of the House during the past year have been simply instruments to advance the political interests of those who have taken part in them, I regret. It has been my pleasure to take part, as it is every man s pleasure and duty to take part, in meetings of that kind, not only in other parts of Canada, but in Ontario. I attended one or two with my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I would just as little think of accusing him of trying to make political capital out of a speech of that kind when appealing to the best instincts of the Canadian people, in a common cause, as he would think of accusing me of trying to make political capital out of such a>
meeting.
While we have had several speeches in which there might be nothing to object to, we have had two speeches to which there has been every reason to object, both as to their tone and their matter. I refer particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Car-vell). We all know our hon. friend from St. John. He is a gentleman who has occupied a prominent position in the coun-' sels of the Liberal party and of the late Government. We know his methods, we know that particularly suave way of his. There is an old saying of a certain man, that the words of his mouth were softer than butter, but war was in his heart. I do not know that the words could be as applicable to anybody else as to my hon. friend from St. John. He is very astute. His methods are of such a kind that he can suggest all sorts of desperate and sinister motives in those whom he politically opposes without coming out flatfooted in such a way as to expose himself to be called to order for transgressing the rules of parliamentary procedure-although he must be accused of coming very near the limit of parliamentary debate on some occasions this session.

The members of this House have long learned to take anything that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., may say with a very large grain of salt. I shall have occasion later on to touch on some of the utterances of my hon. friend; ~as They were directed to myself.
I wish first to refer to a subject which has been freely discussed in this House, which happens to affect me in a rather important way, inasmuch as I am the minister representing the province of British Columbia in this Government, and because, particularly, I happened to be in Victoria on the day that war broke out; and it happened to fall to my lot to have something to do with the purchase of the submarines about which so much discussion has waged in this House. I shall not discuss the evidence, which is bulky, which has been open to the inspection of members on both sides, and which has been extensively quoted from by both the hon. the Solicitor General and the hon. the Minister of Marine. Perhaps the best answer that could be given to either of these members is the answer that was read by the Solicitor General, from the chief Liberal organ in this country, the Toronto Globe. A discussion took place as to the price of these vessels and it fell to my lot to be in Victoria when the matter first came up.

I was asked to go down to the Navy yard by the commanding officer and I went down with Captain Logan. I was there two days running and when the question came up as to the possibility and advisability of getting these submarines at a time when there was critical danger to the coast cities of British Columbia the commanding officer was urging in the strongest way possible that they should be got. Captain Logan, whose testimony is given in the evidence, was comparatively familiar with the type of these vessels, the class to which they belonged and to some extent with their efficiency. He did not know anything about the price. I was standing at the "phone" when Captain Logan asked the agent in Seattle to quote a price if these boats could be procured. My recollection is now-and I think it is pretty clear-that they did not know at Seattle and had to obtain that information from the Electric Boat Company in New York.
